  • Diversify away from dollar dependence
  • Build alternative institutions (BRICS, SCO, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank)
  • Develop independent military capabilities
  • Deepen partnerships with U.S. rivals

  • The Soviet Union spent itself into collapse trying to maintain a coercive sphere

Introduction

For nearly eighty years, the United States has sat atop the global order, possessing the world's most powerful military, its reserve currency, its leading universities, and its most innovative corporations. Washington has subsidized the defense of wealthy allies, tolerated trade practices that hollowed out its industrial base, and extended diplomatic courtesies to regimes that routinely work against American interests. This essay argues that such restraint is a luxury the United States can no longer afford. America should aggressively leverage every instrument of its hegemonic power—military, economic, and diplomatic—to extract maximum advantage for the American people, treating allies and adversaries alike as competitors in a zero-sum contest for prosperity and security.

The Myth of the Benevolent Hegemon

Defenders of the postwar liberal order insist that American magnanimity purchased loyalty and stability. The record suggests otherwise. Germany ran a massive trade surplus with the United States while spending below NATO's two-percent defense target for decades. South Korea and Japan built world-leading industries partly by leveraging privileged access to the American market. Saudi Arabia accepted American security guarantees while coordinating with adversaries to manipulate oil prices. France openly champions "strategic autonomy" whenever it suits Paris. The lesson is clear: gratitude is not a currency that circulates in international politics. States pursue their interests relentlessly, and only those nations willing to impose costs on others are respected.

If allies act as rivals whenever convenient, the United States is entitled—indeed obligated—to reciprocate. A hegemon that refuses to collect rent on the order it underwrites is not benevolent; it is foolish.

The Economic Case for Coercion

American consumers represent the largest single market on Earth. Access to that market is a privilege, not a right, and Washington should price it accordingly. Tariffs, investment screening, export controls, and sanctions are not crude instruments to be deployed apologetically—they are the legitimate tools of a great power.

Consider the dollar. As the global reserve currency, the dollar gives the United States the ability to exclude adversaries from the international financial system with the stroke of a pen. This "weaponized interdependence" has already reshaped the behavior of Iran, Russia, and countless smaller states. Expanding its use—demanding that trading partners align with American sanctions regimes, punishing those who dabble in alternative payment systems, and conditioning market access on favorable trade terms—would convert latent power into realized advantage.

Critics warn of "de-dollarization." Yet every proposed alternative remains marginal precisely because no rival possesses America's combination of deep capital markets, legal institutions, and military reach. The window for aggressive economic statecraft is open now, and hesitation only invites the emergence of alternatives later.

Military Leverage as Diplomatic Currency

The United States spends more on defense than the next ten countries combined. It maintains roughly 750 overseas bases. It is the only nation capable of projecting decisive force to every region of the globe. This unmatched capability is a wasting asset if it is not converted into political and economic gains.

Allies who benefit from American protection should pay for it, in cash and in concessions. If Europe wishes to remain under the American nuclear umbrella, European capitals should accept American terms on trade, technology, and China policy. If Gulf states want American carriers in their waters, they should price their oil accordingly and sever economic ties with American adversaries. If Pacific partners want American deterrence against Beijing, they should open their markets, host American forces on American terms, and align procurement with American defense firms.

This is not cruelty; it is accounting. The bill for global security has always existed. It has simply been paid disproportionately by American taxpayers while the benefits have been distributed internationally. Correcting that imbalance is overdue.

Diplomatic Pressure Without Apology

American diplomats have too often treated international institutions as ends in themselves rather than as venues for advancing American interests. The United Nations, the World Trade Organization, and a host of other bodies consume American resources and legitimacy while frequently producing outcomes contrary to American preferences. Washington should use its influence—its funding, its veto, its convening power—transparently and unsentimentally. Organizations that serve American purposes deserve support. Those that do not deserve defunding, reform, or abandonment.

Bilateral diplomacy should follow the same logic. Visa access, intelligence sharing, technology transfer, and high-level meetings are valuable commodities. Distributing them freely to nations that offer little in return squanders leverage. Distributing them strategically—rewarding alignment, punishing defection—builds a durable coalition of clients who understand that cooperation with Washington pays and defiance costs.

Anticipating the Objections

Opponents will raise several objections. They will argue that aggressive hegemony breeds resentment and balancing coalitions. But the historical record suggests that balancing against the United States has consistently failed precisely because of America's geographic insulation, demographic vitality, and technological edge. States complain but comply.

Others will warn of moral degradation—that a bullying America betrays its founding ideals. The international system rewards power ruthlessly applied and punishes power timidly wielded. The United States stands at a historical apex—militarily preeminent, economically central, diplomatically irreplaceable. To refuse to translate this position into concrete gains for American citizens is not virtue but malpractice. The international system operates in a state of anarchy — not chaos, but the absence of a sovereign authority above nation-states. No world government enforces contracts, punishes aggressors, or guarantees survival. This foundational insight, articulated by thinkers from Thucydides to Hans Morgenthau to John Mearsheimer, yields an inescapable conclusion: in an anarchic system, a state's primary obligation is to itself, and power is the only reliable currency.

Mearsheimer's theory of offensive realism holds that great powers are rationally compelled to maximize their share of world power because no state can ever be certain of another state's intentions. Even allies may become future competitors. Even partners may defect when it suits them. The only reliable guarantee of security and prosperity is overwhelming dominance — a margin of power so vast that no rival or coalition of rivals can credibly challenge American interests.

The United States currently holds this position. The question is whether it will use it or waste it.

Liberal internationalists argue that cooperation, institutions, and norms can substitute for raw power. History repeatedly humiliates this belief. The League of Nations did not prevent World War II. The United Nations could not prevent genocide in Rwanda, ethnic cleansing in the Balkans, or the invasion of Ukraine. International law did not prevent China from militarizing the South China Sea in direct defiance of an international tribunal ruling. Norms are respected only when backed by credible force and ruthless willingness to impose consequences.

The United States should not pretend the world operates on principles it demonstrably does not. It should operate on the principles the world actually runs on — and dominate accordingly.

II. Historical Precedent: Hegemons Who Hesitate Lose

Every great power in history that achieved dominance and then failed to exploit it aggressively was eventually surpassed and diminished. The lesson is consistent across centuries.

The British Empire reached its zenith in the 19th century but gradually adopted a posture of managed decline, believing it could gracefully transfer leadership to multilateral arrangements and allied partnerships. The result was not a peaceful transition but two catastrophic world wars, the loss of its empire, and relegation to a secondary power dependent on American protection.

The Soviet Union matched American power for decades but ultimately collapsed not primarily from external pressure but from an internal unwillingness to extract sufficient surplus from its sphere of influence. It subsidized client states — Cuba, Eastern Europe, various African and Asian regimes — at enormous cost, receiving inadequate strategic return. It treated its empire as an ideological charity rather than an extractive enterprise. It went bankrupt.

Ancient Rome provides the most instructive example. During the Republic and early Empire, Rome ruthlessly exploited its military advantage: it imposed tribute, extracted resources, demanded submission, and punished defiance with devastating force. The result was the Pax Romana — the longest sustained period of relative peace and prosperity in Western history. Rome declined not when it was too aggressive but when it became too accommodating — extending citizenship too broadly, subsidizing frontier peoples rather than subjugating them, allowing military readiness to atrophy in favor of diplomatic accommodation.

The pattern is clear: hegemons that press their advantage create stability through dominance. Hegemons that accommodate create power vacuums that invite chaos. The United States today faces precisely this choice.

America's own history confirms this. The most productive periods of American foreign policy were those characterized by maximum assertiveness: the Monroe Doctrine unilaterally claimed an entire hemisphere; Commodore Perry's gunboat diplomacy forcibly opened Japan to American commerce; the Marshall Plan and Bretton Woods system were not acts of charity but strategic instruments designed to rebuild Europe and Asia along lines favorable to American economic dominance; the Reagan buildup bankrupted the Soviet Union. In each case, America did not ask permission. It imposed terms. And the world was organized to American advantage as a result.

III. The Economic Argument: Wealth Is Extracted, Not Shared

The liberal economic consensus holds that free trade and multilateral economic cooperation produce mutual gains. This is technically true — but strategically irrelevant. The relevant question is not whether cooperation produces gains for all parties but whether the United States is capturing the maximum possible share of those gains.

Consider the present arrangement: The United States provides a global security umbrella — maintaining freedom of navigation in international shipping lanes, deterring aggression against allied nations, and underwriting the stability upon which global commerce depends. This costs American taxpayers approximately $800 billion annually in defense spending. Who benefits? Everyone. Particularly nations like Germany, Japan, South Korea, and the Gulf states, who enjoy American protection while spending a fraction of what the United States does on defense, redirecting those savings into economic competitiveness — often in direct competition with American industries.

This is not partnership. It is exploitation — of the United States.

An aggressive hegemonic strategy would correct this imbalance through several mechanisms:

1. Protection Fees. Allies who benefit from American military protection should pay for it — not at cost-sharing levels politely requested at NATO summits, but at rates that reflect the actual strategic value of the American security guarantee. South Korea, Japan, Germany, and others should be presented with non-negotiable terms: pay substantially or provide for your own defense. The leverage is that no alternative security provider exists. American protection is a monopoly product, and monopolists set prices.

2. Trade Coercion. The United States should use access to the American consumer market — the largest and most valuable in the world — as a weapon, not a gift. Tariffs, import restrictions, and market access should be calibrated not by WTO rules but by what extracts maximum concession from trading partners. China's industrial policy has systematically violated free trade principles for decades through subsidies, intellectual property theft, forced technology transfers, and currency manipulation — while WTO enforcement has proven laughably inadequate. The correct response is not filing disputes in Geneva. It is imposing costs so severe that compliance becomes cheaper than defiance.

3. Dollar Weaponization. The US dollar's status as the world's reserve currency gives America a financial weapon of extraordinary power. The SWIFT system, dollar-denominated debt markets, and the Federal Reserve's influence over global liquidity provide leverage that no other nation possesses. This should be wielded aggressively — sanctioning not only adversaries but any entity, including allied firms and banks, that acts contrary to American economic interests. This is already done selectively (Iran sanctions, for example). It should be done systematically.

4. Resource and Supply Chain Control. The United States should pursue aggressive strategies to control or dominate critical supply chains — rare earth minerals, semiconductors, energy, pharmaceuticals, and agricultural commodities — through a combination of domestic production mandates, strategic stockpiling, and coercing allied nations into exclusive supply arrangements that prioritize American access.

Critics will argue this approach invites retaliation and damages the global economy. This objection misunderstands the power asymmetry. The United States is far less dependent on any single foreign market than any foreign market is dependent on the United States. In any economic confrontation, America holds the stronger hand. The correct strategy when holding the stronger hand is to play it — not fold it in the name of fairness.

IV. The Military Argument: Credible Threats Require Credible Willingness

Military power is the ultimate foundation of hegemonic leverage, but it is only effective when adversaries and allies alike believe the United States is willing to use it — not just in existential self-defense but in pursuit of strategic advantage.

The paradox of military dominance is that it is most effective when it prevents conflict. But deterrence only works if the threat is credible. The moment other nations conclude that the United States will not actually employ force — or will do so only under the most extreme provocation — deterrence collapses, and adversaries are emboldened.

Consider recent history: Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 followed years of American hesitation in Syria, where red lines were drawn and then erased. China's militarization of the South China Sea accelerated during a period of American rhetorical protest but practical inaction. Iran expanded its regional influence through proxy networks while the United States pursued diplomatic accommodation. In each case, the perception of American restraint was interpreted not as virtue but as weakness — and adversaries acted accordingly.

An aggressive hegemonic strategy requires:

1. Forward Deployment and Expansion of Military Presence. The United States should increase, not reduce, its global military footprint, establishing or expanding bases in strategically critical locations — the Indo-Pacific, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Africa — not as defensive measures but as power projection platforms that remind every regional actor of American reach.

2. Explicit and Implicit Threats. Diplomatic language should be less accommodating and more coercive. When the United States demands compliance — whether on trade practices, territorial disputes, or security arrangements — the implicit backdrop of overwhelming military power should be unmistakable. Theodore Roosevelt's dictum of speaking softly while carrying a big stick had it half right. The stick should also be displayed prominently.

3. Punishing Defiance Swiftly and Disproportionately. When any nation — ally or adversary — defies American demands, the response should be swift, disproportionate, and public. This is not cruelty; it is strategic communication. Punishing defiance once, dramatically, reduces the need to do so repeatedly. Conversely, tolerating defiance once invites it perpetually.

4. Maintaining Unchallenged Technological Superiority. The United States should invest whatever is necessary to ensure that no rival approaches parity in military technology — in artificial intelligence, space-based systems, cyber warfare, hypersonic weapons, autonomous systems, and nuclear modernization. Technological dominance is the hardest advantage to replicate and the most decisive in determining outcomes.

V. Handling Allies: Partners Are Not Friends

Perhaps the most counterintuitive element of this strategy is its application to allies. The conventional view holds that allies are strategic assets to be cultivated through partnership, consultation, and shared decision-making. This is naive.

Alliances are transactional arrangements. They exist because they serve mutual interests — but the interests are not equal, and the leverage is not symmetric. The United States does not need NATO as much as NATO needs the United States. Japan's security depends on America far more than America's security depends on Japan. The Gulf states would face existential threats within years without American protection.

This asymmetry should be exploited, not politely ignored.

Allies should be expected to:

  • Align their foreign and economic policies with American priorities, including trade arrangements, technology restrictions, diplomatic votes, and sanctions compliance. Allies who pursue independent policies that conflict with American interests — as France, Germany, and Turkey have periodically done — should face swift economic and diplomatic consequences.

  • Provide basing rights, overflight rights, and logistical support on American terms, not as subjects of negotiation but as conditions of the alliance.

  • Purchase American military equipment as a condition of security cooperation, supporting American defense industries while ensuring interoperability under American command.

  • Subordinate their own diplomatic initiatives in regions where American interests are paramount. European freelancing in the Middle East, Asian allies hedging between Washington and Beijing — these behaviors should incur costs.

The objection will be raised that such treatment will alienate allies and drive them toward rival powers. This objection overestimates allied options. Germany cannot replace American security with Russian or Chinese protection. Japan has no alternative patron. South Korea's geography makes American alliance indispensable. Australia is an island continent dependent on sea lanes only America can guarantee.

When the alternative is nonexistent, the monopolist dictates terms.

VI. Handling Adversaries: Containment Is Insufficient; Subordination Is the Goal

With respect to adversaries — primarily China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea — the goal should not be containment, coexistence, or managed competition. The goal should be strategic subordination: reducing these states to a position where they cannot challenge American interests in any meaningful way.

China is the primary long-term competitor. The correct American strategy is not "decoupling" in the limited sense currently discussed but comprehensive economic, technological, and military pressure designed to slow or reverse China's rise as a peer competitor. This includes:

  • Aggressive restrictions on technology transfer, not just in semiconductors but across all strategic sectors.
  • Organizing allied economies into an exclusive trading bloc that disadvantages Chinese exports.
  • Military posturing in the Indo-Pacific designed to impose maximum strategic stress — including strengthening Taiwan's defenses to the point of effective independence.
  • Economic warfare targeting China's financial system, debt vulnerabilities, and energy dependence.

Russia is a declining power with a nuclear arsenal — dangerous but economically brittle. The strategy should be sustained economic strangulation, energy market manipulation to reduce Russian revenue, and military reinforcement of NATO's eastern flank sufficient to make any Russian adventurism suicidal. The goal is not regime change but permanent strategic irrelevance.

Iran and North Korea are regional nuisances that should be dealt with through maximum pressure campaigns — crippling sanctions, diplomatic isolation, and the credible threat of military action — until they either capitulate on terms favorable to the United States or collapse internally.

VII. The Moral Argument: Stability Through Strength

The most powerful objection to this strategy is moral: that bullying is wrong, that nations have sovereign rights, that the strong should not exploit the weak.

This objection deserves a serious response, and here it is: the alternative is worse.

The 20th century demonstrated twice — in 1914 and 1939 — what happens when no single power dominates the international system. The result is great power competition, arms races, miscalculation, and catastrophic war. The period of greatest global stability, prosperity, and peace in human history — the post-1945 era — coincides precisely with the period of American dominance.

American hegemony has not been perfect, but it has been enormously preferable to any realistic alternative. A world dominated by China would impose authoritarian norms. A multipolar world would reproduce the instability of earlier eras. A world of diminished American power would see proliferation of nuclear weapons, regional arms races, and great power conflicts over spheres of influence.

The moral case for aggressive American hegemony is that it is the least terrible option available. Order is better than chaos. Stability is better than war. And both require a dominant power willing to impose and enforce rules — even when doing so is ugly, coercive, and self-interested.

Moreover, the utilitarian calculus supports this position. American dominance, even self-interested dominance, produces public goods as a byproduct: freedom of navigation, nuclear nonproliferation (however imperfect), containment of regional aggressors, and a global economic system that, whatever its flaws, has lifted billions from poverty. These benefits are incidental to American self-interest, but they are real — and they would evaporate without American power to sustain them.

The moral critic demands that America behave altruistically. But altruism unsupported by power is impotent, and power exercised altruistically is power wasted. The United States can do far more good for the world by remaining overwhelmingly dominant — and ruthlessly self-interested — than by constraining itself in deference to principles that no other great power in history has ever observed.

VIII. Addressing Counterarguments

"This will provoke anti-American coalitions." Theoretically possible. In practice, balancing coalitions are extraordinarily difficult to form and sustain. China and Russia are deeply suspicious of each other. European nations cannot agree on basic fiscal policy, let alone a unified anti-American front. The historical record shows that balancing against a hegemon almost never succeeds as long as the hegemon maintains decisive military and economic advantages. And America's advantages are not marginal — they are overwhelming.

"This is imperialism." Imperialism involves the direct governance of foreign peoples. This strategy does not require territorial acquisition or political administration. It requires compliance. There is a meaningful distinction between ruling a nation and demanding favorable terms from it.

"This will destroy the liberal international order." The liberal international order is already fracturing — under the weight of Chinese revisionism, Russian aggression, institutional sclerosis, and the failure of multilateral bodies to enforce their own rules. Clinging to an eroding order is not strategy; it is nostalgia. Better to build a new order explicitly organized around American power than to mourn the loss of one that depended on American power all along but pretended otherwise.

"Public opinion won't support it." The American public has consistently supported assertive foreign policy when it is framed in terms of concrete national interest — jobs, security, economic competitiveness. What the public does not support is military adventurism without clear benefit (Iraq, Afghanistan) or subsidizing allies who don't contribute their fair share. An aggressive hegemonic strategy aligned with visible economic and security benefits would command significant public support.

"Other nations have rights and sovereignty." Sovereignty is a legal fiction sustained by power. In the international system, sovereignty means the ability to resist coercion. Nations with the power to resist can do so. Nations without that power have always been subject to the demands of stronger states. This has been the reality of international politics for millennia. Pretending otherwise is not morality — it is self-deception.

Conclusion

The United States stands at a historical inflection point. Its margin of dominance, while still vast, is narrowing as China rises, Russia disrupts, and the international order frays. The window during which America can leverage its unmatched power to lock in maximum long-term advantage is finite.

The strategic imperative is clear: use the advantage now, while it exists, as aggressively and comprehensively as possible. Extract maximum economic concessions from trading partners. Demand maximum contributions from allies. Impose maximum costs on adversaries. Maintain military dominance so overwhelming that challenges are unthinkable. Weaponize the dollar, the consumer market, technology access, and security guarantees without apology.

This is not a call for recklessness. It is a call for ruthless strategic calculation — the kind practiced by every great power that successfully sustained its dominance. The United States has been, by historical standards, an extraordinarily benevolent hegemon. It has subsidized allies, opened its markets, rebuilt former enemies, and poured blood and treasure into maintaining a global order from which it has undercharged and from which others have profited disproportionately.

That era of strategic generosity should end.

Not because generosity is wrong in principle, but because the international system does not reward generosity. It rewards power, exercised decisively, in the service of interest. The United States has the power. It has the interest. What it has lacked is the will.

The argument of this essay is that it should find that will — before the opportunity passes, the advantage erodes, and history renders its unflinching judgment on a hegemon that had everything and squandered it in pursuit of applause it was never going to receive.
